body: {"total":6,"records":[{"title":"Prevalence of financial toxicity among adults receiving systemic cancer therapy: a five-centre survey with a validated 11-item questionnaire","authors":"Mensah-Kowalski A, Lindqvist-Obi J, Carvalho-Stroud E","year":2021,"venue":"Ashcombe Supportive Oncology Care","doi":"10.5555/jsoc.2021.0263","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed 1,450 adults receiving systemic therapy in five cancer centres with a validated financial toxicity questionnaire; 64 percent of those approached responded. Thirty-eight percent reported moderate or severe financial toxicity. Financial toxicity was more common among patients under 65, those with household income in the lowest two quintiles, those who had stopped working because of treatment and those living more than 50 kilometres from the centre. Patients receiving oral targeted therapy reported higher out-of-pocket spending on medicines. Non-respondents were younger and more often lived far from the centre, so the prevalence may be underestimated."},{"title":"Out-of-pocket costs and travel burden during chemotherapy: a patient diary study","authors":"Achterberg-Nwosu D, Fairclough-Sato M","year":2019,"venue":"Cancer Care Economics Notes","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two hundred and twelve patients receiving chemotherapy kept a spending diary for twelve weeks. Travel and parking made up 41 percent of out-of-pocket spending, medicines and supplements 27 percent and lost income of family carers was reported by a third of patients. Patients living in rural areas spent on average twice as much on travel as those living in the city. Spending was highest in the first six weeks of treatment. The authors note that diary completion fell over time, especially among patients who were most unwell."},{"title":"Agreement between a single financial distress item and a multi-item financial toxicity score in oncology outpatients","authors":"Brennan-Oyelowo S, Haddad-Lund P, Tanaka-Achebe V","year":2023,"venue":"Wrenmouth Cancer Distress Measurement Reports","doi":"10.5555/pomr.2023.0088","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"In 640 oncology outpatients we compared a single financial problems item from a distress screening checklist with a validated multi-item financial toxicity score. The single item identified 61 percent of patients with moderate or severe financial toxicity on the multi-item score, and agreement beyond chance was moderate (kappa 0.45). Patients who did not tick the item despite high scores were more often older and more often described money as a private matter. The authors suggest that a single checkbox can support but not replace a short validated measure."},{"title":"Non-response in cancer patient surveys: who is missed and does it matter?","authors":"Olawale-Petersen K, Moreau-Ibrahim L","year":2020,"venue":"Survey Methods in Oncology","doi":"10.5555/smo.2020.0041","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Across four surveys of cancer patients, non-respondents were younger, had lower incomes and more often spoke a language other than the survey language. Offering the questionnaire in several modes (paper, tablet and telephone) and in the main community languages raised response from 48 to 66 percent and reduced the difference in response between income groups by half. Estimates of unmet need changed by up to eight percentage points when weighting for non-response. The authors recommend recording the characteristics of everyone approached so that non-response can be described and weighted."},{"title":"Financial toxicity and skipped or delayed cancer treatment: a systematic review of 19 observational studies","authors":"Kagame-Whitlock R, Sorensen-Mbatha T","year":2022,"venue":"Supportive Care Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/scer.2022.0192","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 19 observational studies examining financial toxicity and adherence to cancer treatment. Across studies, patients with financial toxicity more often skipped doses, delayed treatment or missed appointments (pooled odds ratio 1.8, 95 percent CI 1.4 to 2.3), with substantial heterogeneity. Most studies were cross-sectional, so the direction of the association is uncertain, and adherence was usually self-reported. No study tested whether screening followed by financial navigation improved adherence. The authors call for routine measurement of financial toxicity with a validated instrument."},{"title":"Financial navigation in cancer centres: a before-after evaluation of a navigator service","authors":"Petrov-Adeyemi M, Lindgren-Castellanos H","year":2024,"venue":"Ashcombe Supportive Oncology Care","doi":"10.5555/jsoc.2024.0017","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One cancer centre introduced a financial navigator who helped patients with benefits, travel grants and medicine costs. Among 310 patients who used the service, median out-of-pocket spending over three months fell by 38 percent and the mean financial toxicity score improved modestly. Patients referred through distress screening were less likely to be the most affected than those referred by social workers. The navigator saw a median of three patients a day, and waiting times for a first appointment rose to three weeks by the end of the year. The evaluation had no comparison group and patients chose whether to use the service."}]}
